classification.difficultyReason: Use the mean to find the sum of two missing integers, then apply strict ordering to enumerate all possible pairs.

content.prompt: The numbers $5, 12, 16, x, y, 24, 30$ have mean $18$. If $x$ and $y$ are positive integers and the numbers are arranged from smallest to largest with no two numbers the same, find the possible values of $x$ and $y$.

answer.short:
$(x,y)=(17,22),\ (18,21),\ (19,20)$.

The missing numbers sum to $39$ and satisfy $16<x<y<24$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Sum of all seven numbers}&=7\times18=126\\\text{Sum of the known numbers}&=5+12+16+24+30=87\\x+y&=126-87\\x+y&=39\end{align*}$$

The stated order and distinct values require $16<x<y<24$. Since $x<y$ and their sum is $39$, $x$ can only be $17$, $18$ or $19$.

$$\begin{aligned}x=17:&\quad y=39-17=22\\x=18:&\quad y=39-18=21\\x=19:&\quad y=39-19=20\end{aligned}$$

Thus the possible pairs are $(17,22)$, $(18,21)$ and $(19,20)$. Each pair satisfies the strict order and gives a total of $126$, so the mean is $18$.

inlines.text: Why are these the only regular polygons that tessellate by themselves?

Use a template to show what happens when you try to use a different regular polygon – such as a pentagon, an octagon or a nonagon – to tessellate the plane. Copy and complete this table of the sizes of interior angles. Then explain why the equilateral triangle, square and hexagon are the only regular polygons that can be used by themselves to tessellate.
Six equilateral triangles, four squares or three regular hexagons meet at a vertex, making exactly
. The other regular polygons leave gaps or overlap.

answer.worked:
For an $n$-sided polygon, the interior angle sum is $(n-2)\times180^{\circ}$. Divide by $n$ for each angle of a regular polygon.

$\begin{aligned}I_3&=180^{\circ}\div3=60^{\circ}\\I_4&=360^{\circ}\div4=90^{\circ}\\I_5&=540^{\circ}\div5=108^{\circ}\\I_6&=720^{\circ}\div6=120^{\circ}\\I_7&=900^{\circ}\div7=128\frac47^{\circ}\\I_8&=1080^{\circ}\div8=135^{\circ}\\I_9&=1260^{\circ}\div9=140^{\circ}\\I_{10}&=1440^{\circ}\div10=144^{\circ}\\I_{12}&=1800^{\circ}\div12=150^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

Place congruent templates edge to edge around a common vertex. Three pentagons occupy $324^{\circ}$, leaving $36^{\circ}$; a fourth overlaps. Two octagons occupy $270^{\circ}$, leaving $90^{\circ}$; a third overlaps. Two nonagons occupy $280^{\circ}$, leaving $80^{\circ}$; a third overlaps.

Angles at a point must total $360^{\circ}$ without gaps or overlaps:

$\begin{aligned}6\times60^{\circ}&=360^{\circ}\\4\times90^{\circ}&=360^{\circ}\\3\times120^{\circ}&=360^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

The pentagon's $108^{\circ}$ does not divide $360^{\circ}$ exactly. Every regular polygon with more than six sides has an interior angle greater than $120^{\circ}$ and less than $180^{\circ}$: two leave a gap and three overlap. Therefore only equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons tessellate by themselves.

answer.worked: Construct $AB$ and its midpoint $M$. Draw the two $45^\circ$ rays. With compass radius $AB$, locate $E$ on the left ray from centre $A$ and $C$ on the right ray from centre $B$. answer.short: Four tiles form the elongated hexagon shown, and copies of that hexagon tile the plane without gaps or overlaps.
answer.worked:
The interior angles of a pentagon sum to $540^\circ$. Since $C=E=90^\circ$,
$$\begin{align*}A+B+D&=540^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ\\A+B+D&=360^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus the three labelled angles fit around each central junction. The paired right angles make straight outer edges. Four pentagons form the elongated hexagon shown; translated copies of this hexagon cover the plane.

entries.description:
We will begin with tessellations that can be created using just one polygon. If we limit ourselves to regular polygons, there are only three possibilities:
1 equilateral triangles will tessellate
2 squares will tessellate
3 regular hexagons will tessellate.
The resulting patterns are called the regular tessellations.

entries.description:
The Cairo tessellation is so named because tiles such as these were used for many years on the streets of Cairo. Each tile is a pentagon with all sides of equal length.
Note that this pentagon is not regular, even though its sides are of equal length, because it does not have all its interior angles of the same size.
You can draw one such tile using your protractor, ruler and compasses.
Step 1: Draw the interval AB.
Step 2: Find the midpoint M of AB.
Step 3: Draw rays from M at 45° to AB.
Step 4: Use your compasses set at the length of AB to complete the pentagon.
The angles of the pentagon at E and C are 90°.
Draw one of these pentagons on card. Use it to form the Cairo tessellation.
Why does this pentagon tessellate?
Another way of drawing such a pentagon is suggested by the diagram shown. Draw two identical right-angled isosceles triangles on card. Cut them out, join them at D as shown, and rotate one around D so that AB is the same length as the equal sides of the isosceles triangles.

entries.description:
After Activity 1, you probably noticed that, because the angles about a point add up to 360°, there are some combinations of regular polygons that can be used to tessellate the plane. These are called semiregular tessellations. One way of describing them is to look at the set of regular polygons that meet at a point and write down the numbers of sides these polygons have, in ‘cyclic order’ (that is, clockwise starting from the highest number), in square brackets. For example, the code for the second tessellation shown below is [6, 4, 3, 4].

Write the codes for the other seven semiregular tessellations.
